A '''simple point process''' is a special type of [[point process]] in [[probability theory]]. In simple point processes, every point is assigned the weight one.

== Definition ==
Let <math> S </math> be a [[Locally compact space|locally compact]] [[Second-countable space|second countable]] [[Hausdorff space]] and let <math> \mathcal S </math> be its [[Borel set|Borel <math> \sigma </math>-algebra]]. A [[point process]] <math> \xi </math>, interpreted as [[random measure]] on <math> (S, \mathcal S) </math>, is called a simple point process if it can be written as
:<math> \xi =\sum_{i \in I} \delta_{X_i} </math>

for an [[index set]] <math> I </math> and [[random element]]s <math> X_i </math> which are almost everywhere pairwise distinct. Here <math> \delta_x </math> denotes the [[Dirac measure]] on the point <math> x </math>.

== Examples ==
Simple point processes include many important classes of point processes such as [[Poisson process]]es, [[Cox process]]es and [[binomial process]]es.

== Uniqueness ==
If <math> \mathcal I </math> is a generating [[Ring of sets|ring]] of <math> \mathcal S </math> then a simple point process <math> \xi </math> is uniquely determined by its values on the sets <math> U \in \mathcal I </math>. This means that two simple point processes <math> \xi </math> and <math> \zeta </math> have the same distributions iff
:<math> P(\xi(U)=0) = P(\zeta(U)=0) \text{ for all } U \in \mathcal I</math>
